Subject: First-emit targets and streaming behavior — discovery recap & pilot asks

Alex / Priya — thanks again for a productive call. Quick recap and a set of concrete asks so we can scope a focused pilot.

High-level from the call
- Primary goal: reduce perceived latency in our live product when users request multi-turn summaries. Target UX: user sees first content within ~150-220ms after request is accepted.
- Traffic profile: peak concurrency estimated 350-500 concurrent chat sessions during peak (US region). Average request size ~120 tokens in prompt, expected generated length ~80-200 tokens.
- Reliability: must sustain bursts of +2x baseline for 10min windows without error-rate spike.

Open technical clarifications (what we need from you)
1) Can you confirm the front-end connection preference for streaming? You flagged SSE in the call but mentioned WebSocket fallback. We want to understand browser support constraints and how you plan to handle multiplexing.
2) Acceptable chunk cadence — do you prefer many small chunks (e.g., 50-100ms cadence) or fewer bigger chunks (200-400ms cadence) for the UI? This affects TTFT numbers and server CPU patterns.
3) Expected per-minute QPS for pilot (estimate a small user cohort). For capacity planning we need a sample traffic file or the typical per-minute request counts.
4) Any restrictions on model variants (quantized vs fp16) for acceptable quality during pilot?

Proposed Redwood pilot deliverables
- 2-week pilot: controlled traffic ramp with defined traffic steps (we’ll supply a small harness).
- Measured metrics: TTFT (p50/p90), per-token latency, error rate, concurrency vs latency curve.
- Two streaming modes tested: SSE primary path, WebSocket fallback.
- Suggested acceptance criteria: p90 TTFT <= 300ms under nominal load (200 concurrent), error rate <1%.

Attachments: pilot matrix (redwood-ttft-pilot-matrix.xlsx) and a short note on streaming tradeoffs.

Next steps (action items)
- Alex: share expected pilot QPS and any sample traffic traces by EOD Tue (June 15).
- Priya: confirm whether the front-end team can accept SSE or need WS-only by Tue.
- Ben / Karthik: we’ll follow with a short tech note on chunk cadence tradeoffs and a proposed test harness.

Thanks — I’ll schedule a 30-min pilot kickoff for Thu if we have the artifacts.

Best,
Hannah

Hannah / Alex / Priya — quick tech clarifications from my side, plus a suggested default test configuration.

SSE vs WebSocket
- SSE is simpler for single-stream-to-client flows and integrates with existing browser EventSource APIs. It suffers with intermediate proxies that buffer; we'll include heartbeat frames and small prefix chunks to mitigate buffering.
- WebSocket is preferable if you plan to multiplex multiple distinct streams over one connection (e.g., many chat windows per tab). WS gives lower overhead for many small messages.

Chunk cadence tradeoffs
- Small chunks (~50-100ms cadence): better perceived freshness but increases CPU interrupts and makes batching less efficient. TTFT might be slightly better for small prompts but cost goes up.
- Medium chunks (150-300ms): good tradeoff — reduces syscall overhead, preserves strong TTFT for typical responses.
- Large chunks (>400ms): less responsive UI, better throughput/cost.

Suggested pilot defaults (we can tune after first run)
- Streaming mode: SSE primary, WebSocket fallback. Use SSE with 150-250ms chunk cadence.
- Model: start with a 4-bit-quantized variant for base runs to stress cost; run quality check at p50/p90 tokens against your golden prompts. If quality drops, switch to fp16 for comparison.
- Concurrency test: ramp 0 -> 250 -> 500 concurrent sessions in 15-minute steps. Track p50/p90 TTFT and per-token latency.

Data we need from Streamly / ClearCart
- Sample 20-minute trace at a representative hour (JSON list: timestamp + request size + session id). If you can’t share raw traces, provide per-minute counts for the desired test window.
- Indicate whether clients will reuse long-lived connections across multiple requests (important for warm KV-cache behavior).

I attached a short note (sse-vs-ws-recommendation.pdf) with diagrams and a proposed chunk scheduler. I’ll also prepare a small harness script for the pilot.

-Ben
Ben Carter | Principal Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: First-emit targets and streaming behavior — discovery recap & pilot asks

Thanks Hannah / Ben — appreciate the clear notes. Quick answers from our side:

1) Front-end connection: our current web app uses a WS-based wrapper for older browsers (legacy support). However we can accept SSE for modern clients if Redwood provides a stable SSE path; default for the pilot should be WS so we don’t have to change client infra.
2) Chunk cadence: we prefer medium chunks (150-300ms). Our UX team reported that too-frequent small updates cause layout thrashing on mobile.
3) Pilot QPS: for the initial cohort expect 18 requests/minute average per 50 users. For the 50-user pilot that’s ~900 requests/minute peak. We can provide a short JSON trace by EOD Tue (June 15).
4) Model variants: initial pilot must match production quality. We can accept a quantized run only if you run A/B checks vs fp16 and we see no regression on our golden prompts.

Concerns
- Warm-up: we will likely open many long-lived WS connections but request less frequently per connection; important that KV-cache warmstart works as you measure.
- Bursts: we may have short marketing bursts that double traffic for 3–8 minutes; we need graceful degradation policies.

We’ll send the trace and a short list of golden prompts. If WS is default for the pilot, can you still run SSE as a comparison on the backend?

—Alex
Product Manager, Streamly
